power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: The human face affords a remarkable array of complex social cues, yet our understanding of how it is spontaneously perceived relies almost exclusively on controlled, posed stimuli that suppress the natural variation which makes faces so informative.
Here, using a data-driven similarity task with 75 naturalistic face images, we mapped 182,500 perceptual judgments across 365 adults aged 20 to 76.

The results indicated that naturalistic face space was hierarchically organized by expressive and demographic cues: smiling faces formed a coherent category that transcended gender and age, whereas non-smiling adult faces stratified along apparent gender.

Representational similarity analysis showed that affective dimensions (valence, intensity, energy), emotion category, demographic cues (age and gender), and image-based color each uniquely predicted similarity judgments, while specific personality traits and facial action unit intensity did not.

These results demonstrate that highly variable naturalistic faces carry potent combinations of both categorical and dimensional information, advancing a more ecologically valid framework for understanding real-world social perception.
Making sense of the faces we see is an extraordinary feat.

From a deceptively simple configuration of facial attributes, even the faces of strangers convey vast quantities of information, such as age, gender, identity, physiological state, personality traits, emotional appeals, and conversational intent (Buckland & Taubert, 2025; Cowen & Keltner, 2020; Holler, 2025; Leung et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2022; Scarantino et al., 2022; Sutherland & Young, 2022; White & Burton, 2022).

text.text: To extract this multidimensional information, the brain is thought to compare incoming facial attributes against stored mental representations (Valentine et al., 2016).
text.formatted: To extract this multidimensional information, the brain is thought to compare incoming facial attributes against stored mental representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Valentine et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: To isolate specific mechanisms, previous research has traditionally relied on tightly controlled face stimuli, varying attributes along isolated dimensions, such as identity, expression, gaze or face shape, while holding all other facial attributes constant.

While such studies have provided foundational insights into how faces are categorized (Bruce et al., 1987; Bruce & Young, 1986; Porcheron et al., 2013; Rossion, 2002; Taubert et al., 2016), recognized (Taubert & Alais, 2011; Towler et al., 2023; White & Burton, 2022), elicit social inferences (Barrett et al., 2019; Fujimura et al., 2012; Russell, 1980), and guide predictions (Chanes et al., 2018), they necessarily restrict sampling to a curated subset of representational space.
text.formatted: While such studies have provided foundational insights into how faces are categorized <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bruce et al., 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Bruce & Young, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Porcheron et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Rossion, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Taubert et al., 2016)</ref>, recognized <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Taubert & Alais, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Towler et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">White & Burton, 2022)</ref>, elicit social inferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barrett et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Fujimura et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Russell, 1980)</ref>, and guide predictions <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chanes et al., 2018)</ref>, they necessarily restrict sampling to a curated subset of representational space.

text.text: Consequently, these paradigms may not fully account for the variable and flexible feature integration characteristic of facial information 'in the wild'.

Further, traditional methods for eliciting behavioral judgments typically assess performance using categorization or recognition tasks, which make it difficult to elicit behavioral judgments without biasing responses toward predefined dimensions.

For example, facial emotion recognition paradigms often rely on prototypical emotion categories (happiness, anger, fear, disgust, sadness, and surprise) represented by distinct configurations of facial action units (AUs) (Ekman & Friesen, 1978).
text.formatted: For example, facial emotion recognition paradigms often rely on prototypical emotion categories (happiness, anger, fear, disgust, sadness, and surprise) represented by distinct configurations of facial action units (AUs) <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Ekman & Friesen, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: Stimuli are typically controlled for these activations and paired with corresponding labels to assess behavior in laboratory settings.

While highly valuable for establishing baseline mechanisms, this approach necessarily leaves aside non-prototypical AU configurations and constrains the diversity of descriptive MULTIDIMENSIONAL REPRESENTATIONS OF NATURALISTIC FACES labels available to participants.

Restricting response options in this way has been shown to influence performance, by potentially inflating consensus (Adams & Weisbuch, 2026; Nelson & Russell, 2013), limiting observations to predefined categories (Betz et al., 2019; Lindquist & Gendron, 2013), and/or privileging singular dimensions over latent, complex, or contradictory social cues (Matsumoto & Wilson, 2026).

text.text: Because natural faces reflect multiple interacting dimensions, constrained approaches risk inadvertently reinforcing the theoretical commitments they intend to test (Peluso et al., 2025).

text.text: Consequently, less is known about how mental representations of naturalistic faces are organized when facial signals retain information traditionally treated as noise.

More recently, data-driven methods have emerged for assessing perceptual face similarity in an unbiased way, making it possible to use larger and more complex stimulus sets which seek to explain face perception under more ecologically valid conditions.
Here, our goal was to use one such method to characterize the multidimensional representations underlying a set of "uncontrolled" faces without imposing a facial attribute of interest.

To this end, we quantified perceptual similarity using a triplet odd-one-out task previously used to understand latent dimensions in objects (Grootswagers et al., 2024; Hebart et al., 2020) with the Wild Faces Database (Peluso, Long et al., 2023), a diverse collection of ambient images displaying a range of heterogeneous facial gestures.

text.text: The triplet odd-one-out task presents three stimuli simultaneously, with the participant choosing the one that is most different.

No further instructions are provided to avoid biasing attention to any singular dimension, allowing the task to reveal similarities which might otherwise remain latent without presupposing or labeling the attributes of interest in advance.

In order to characterize the multidimensional space revealed by this paradigm, we separately collected behavioral ratings for 75 Wild Face images, consisting of 70 human faces (35 male, 31 female, four ambiguous) and five illusory faces (pareidolia), which we retained given evidence that perceiving face-ness in objects influences the perception of social cues such as valence and gender (Saurels et al., MULTIDIMENSIONAL REPRESENTATIONS OF NATURALISTIC FACES 2024; Taubert et al., 2023; Wardle et al., 2022).

text.text: Crucially, we identify a remarkably robust geometry underlying naturalistic face similarity judgements, scaffolded by interpretable and flexible combinations of affective dimensions and social categories.
The results provide an important and necessary step toward an ecologically informed model for describing how humans make sense of faces in the real world.

text.text: For each pair of faces, similarity was computed as the proportion of trials where the pair appeared together and neither image was selected as the odd one out, divided by the total number of trials that included that pair.
These similarity scores were then subtracted from 1 for conversion into dissimilarity scores, such that higher values indicated pairs were perceived as more different.
Dissimilarity scores were calculated for all pairs of 75 stimuli, resulting in a 75 x 75 Representational Dissimilarity Matrix (RDM) comprising 2,775 unique pairs.

We also used RSA to compute the split-half consensus of similarity judgments across participants by randomly dividing participants into two groups and correlating their RDMs across 1,000 bootstrap iterations.
Using the same bootstrap method, we also assessed between-trial reliability by dividing trials into odd-and even-indexed halves, retaining the full N in each half.
Correlations were corrected using the Spearman-Brown formula.

We built multiple model RDMs for perceived age, attentiveness, attractiveness, energy, familiarity, gaze, gender, genuineness, intensity, likeability, trustworthiness and valence by computing pairwise dissimilarity as the absolute difference between the two faces' mean ratings (using city-block distance, which for a single rating dimension is identical to Euclidean distance).
The emotion category RDM was constructed using dissimilarity in the rated emotional profile of each face.

First, for all 75 faces we constructed a 9 x 1 vector based on the proportion of raters who selected each emotion category label (anger, fear, disgust, sadness, neutral, happiness, surprise, other or unknown) for each face in a previous labeling task (Peluso, Long et al., 2023).

We used multiple regression on RDM distance matrices to estimate each candidate model's unique contribution to behavioral similarity with all other models held constant.

The behavioral RDM for all participants was vectorized and regressed simultaneously onto the corresponding vectors from each of our candidate models as predictors, yielding standardized regression coefficients (β) reflecting each model's unique contribution after partialling out shared variance.
One challenge with inference using RSA is that observations within an RDM are not independent.

We therefore followed a stimulus-label randomisation approach (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Nili et al., 2014) and combined this exchangeability method with the Freedman-Lane procedure (Winkler et al., 2014), under which each predictor is tested against a null that retains the effects of the remaining predictors.

We used Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) to map the underlying structure of the behavioral RDM, such that faces perceived as more similar are positioned closer to each other in space than faces perceived as more different (Kruskal & Wish, 1978).

text.text: To assess the optimal number of dimensions, we computed MDS solutions from 2 -8 dimensions using Kruskal's Stress 1 formula to measure fit quality, achieving stress 0.077 by seven dimensions but with no clear elbow (see Supplementary Fig. 1).

text.text: Given improvement dropped to ~1.2% between seven and eight dimensions, we retained the sevendimensional (7D) solution as an optimal balance between preserving meaningful structure while retaining interpretability.
We applied hierarchical clustering (average linkage) using the pairwise Euclidean distances derived from the 7D MDS embedding using MATLAB 2025b.
Average linkage defines the similarity between two clusters as the average distance between all possible pairs of observations across the two groups.
Given naturalistic face stimuli are more perceptually graded, this algorithm was chosen for its robustness to outliers and to preserve the geometric structure of the underlying pairwise distances.

We evaluated the optimal number of clusters by computing mean silhouette width for solutions from k = 2 to 10, using Euclidean distances in the same seven-dimensional space in which the clustering was performed.

Silhouette width was maximal for the trivial two-cluster solution (s̄ = .35), which separated the five pareidolia stimuli from the remaining faces, while in the range of human faces silhouette width rose from a minimum at k = 3 (s̄ = .20) to a maximum at k = 7 (s̄ = .29), with k = 8 closely comparable (s̄ = .28) before plateauing to k = 10 (s̄ = .28).

Given the graded nature of the silhouette values, we also examined the merge heights of the dendrogram itself, where two face images high in similarity are located in close proximity and connected by vertical branches which are low in height.
Excluding the human/pareidolia cluster split (gap = .185), the largest increases occurred at k = 4 (gap = .055) and k = 8 (gap = .044); no other solution exceeded .025.
We therefore converged upon an eight-cluster solution which explained 66.59% of the total variance in the 7D MDS space, representing a robust clustering solution with strong overall separation.
Clusters were profiled using the independent ratings data and OpenFace 2.0 using RStudio 2026.01.1+403.

We quantified consensus among participants using split-half reliability and found similarity judgments were remarkably consistent both across participants (r = .968) and across trials (r = .969), Spearman-Brown corrected.

Given the equitable distribution of female and male participants within the MULTIDIMENSIONAL REPRESENTATIONS OF NATURALISTIC FACES full sample (n = 182 each), we also quantified consensus within and between each gender group which we found to be similarly high (females: across-participants, r = .938 and across-trials, r = .946; males: across-participants, r = .936 and across-trials, r = .939).
Similarly, the behavioral RDMs that were generated by male and female participants were highly correlated with each other (Spearman's rho r = .92, p < .001).

Each age RDM contained 40-43 participants, each covering 100% of 2,775 pairwise comparisons with a median count of 21-23 observations.

Despite the relative sparsity in these RDMs compared to the full sample RDM (which contained a median count of 149-197 observations per pair), consensus remained strong with all age groups significantly correlated with each other, ranging between rs = .697 and .764, p < .001, FDR corrected.

text.text: After establishing impressive agreement between participants as to which faces were more similar than others, we next sought to identify which of our socio-evaluative ratings and stimulusderived computational models might independently predict these judgments using multiple regression.

Given our task included illusory faces (i.e., pareidolia) which do not feature facial action units and may contain contrasting visual statistics to human faces (such as luminance and color), we conducted three separate analyses: the first included all 75 stimuli (70 human faces and 5 pareidolia) with 17 predictors, excluding OpenFace.

The second introduced OpenFace and excluded six stimuli OpenFace could not process (five pareidolia stimuli and one black-and-white human face), yielding a 69-face dataset with the full 18-predictor set.

Given Analyses One and Two differed in both stimulus set and predictor set, Analysis Three was fitted on the 69-face dataset with the same predictors as Analysis One to be able to compare the effect of stimulus removal separately to the inclusion of OpenFace.

Overall model fit was MULTIDIMENSIONAL REPRESENTATIONS OF NATURALISTIC FACES significant in all three analyses (permutation p < .001; R² = .351, .371, and .369, respectively), corresponding to approximately 36-39% of the explainable variance given the noise ceiling (R² = .969 and .957 for 75 and 69 stimuli).

This suggests that the genuineness and color effects in Analysis One may partly reflect the perceptual distinction between human and illusory faces.

Together, these results indicate that naturalistic face similarity is predicted by a combination of expressive (valence, emotion category, intensity, energy), demographic (age, gender), and image-level (luminance, color) dimensions.

text.text: Our results so far reveal naturalistic faces elicit high-dimensional and remarkably consistent similarity judgments which are uniquely predicted by expressive, demographic, and image-level cues.

To identify the face attributes underlying these dimensions, we used hierarchical clustering as a means of recovering categorical structure while preserving dimensionality, grouping stimuli solely on the basis of their pairwise dissimilarities.

Figure 3 displays the full clustering solution as a vertical dendrogram alongside the RDM arranged in the order of images derived from hierarchical clustering, revealing highly distinct clusters of low dissimilarity along the diagonal (dark blue).

text.text: Pareidolia images (n = 5) emerged as the most distinct cluster and were judged as strongly dissimilar to human faces, visible as a high dissimilarity (yellow) horizontal stripe along the bottom of the RDM.
Accordingly, if the resulting clusters are interpretable, then face images should share certain identifiable properties that might explain category membership.

text.text: We describe these groups in terms of their shared features.

The most distinct cluster (n = 5, blue) contained all face pareidolia images (Fig. 4, top), indicating a strong categorical boundary between human faces and illusory faces in objects which emerged at the highest branching point of the dendrogram (~0.8).

text.text: Among human faces, the most distinct cluster contained images of children/babies (n = 7, cyan) irrespective of variability on other dimensions (e.g. gender, facial gesture).
Indeed, mean attributed age for this group of stimuli was 5.67 (SD = 1.84) in comparison to the mean age of the remaining stimuli (which ranged from 21.86 -39.14).
Interestingly, older faces did not similarly form a unique cluster, but were distributed into other adult clusters, suggesting an asymmetry in how age information is combined with other social cues.

Cluster three revealed a uniquely coherent category for smiles (n = 12, green) which transcended variations in stable demographic cues such as gender, ethnicity, and age, and highly variable cues such as gaze direction and MULTIDIMENSIONAL REPRESENTATIONS OF NATURALISTIC FACES head orientation.

Remaining clusters were organized by salient non-smiling facial gestures (n = 13, teal), faces with hands covering mouths (n = 3, orange), or by gender and/or ethnicity (n = 11, red; n = 15, vermillion; n = 9, purple).

Interestingly, while the perceived gender and ethnicity of face stimuli seemed robust organizers of clusters six to eight, these cues also seemed important within clusters two to five, with faces from the same gender or ethnicity tending to be proximal to each other.

While cluster three (smiles, n = 12) was notably coherent across both AU12 (Lip corner puller, CV = 0.5) and AU06 (Cheek raiser, CV = 0.5) -activations thought crucial for so-called genuine or Duchenne smiles -cluster five (n = 3) also revealed similar specificity across several mouth-related AUs including AU14 (Dimpler, CV = 0.5), AU07 (Lid tightener, CV = 0.6), and AU20 (Lip stretcher, CV = 0.3) despite these images all containing faces with hands covering the mouth region.

This confusability suggests challenges remain in detecting AUs in naturalistic face stimuli, and that naturalistic face stimuli may contain more complex combinations of AUs than basic emotion category models predict.

In this study we combined an unbiased measure of perceived similarity, data-driven multivariate analyses, and independent perceptual and socio-evaluative explanatory models, to map the similarity across 75 naturalistic face images, allowing the stimuli to freely vary without specifying in advance which dimensions should matter.
Three major findings emerged.

First, we found impressive agreement in how observers spontaneously responded to highly variable naturalistic facial attributes across the adult lifespan, even without providing explicit instructions.

Second, we found that models evaluating the expressive (valence, emotion category, intensity, energy), demographic (facial age, gender), and imagelevel (luminance, color) dimensions of naturalistic faces partially captured this representational geometry.

Third, we found these dimensions were flexibly combined to structure the underlying multidimensionality of naturalistic face space; cues consistent with facial age and gender provided pronounced categorical structure, yet smiles were elevated to cut across these stable demographic MULTIDIMENSIONAL REPRESENTATIONS OF NATURALISTIC FACES cues.

Together, these findings reveal a hierarchically organized yet context-sensitive geometry for incorporating multiple behaviorally relevant social cues in naturalistic faces, with important consequences for understanding the foundations underlying human face perception.

That observers spontaneously extracted multiplexed social categories and dimensions from uncontrolled naturalistic faces is consistent with a contextually sensitive process for integrating social affordances from stable and expressive facial attributes using more controlled stimuli (Baudouin et al., 2025; Fujimura et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2022; Mehu and Scherer 2015).

text.text: Here, we extend this work to reveal that categories such as gender, age, and emotion were not uniformly defined across naturalistic face space but rather interacted differently depending on the presence or absence of salient expressive cues.

Further, dimensions of intensity and energy were not orthogonal to bipolar valence but instead appeared dependent, consistent with a V-shaped relationship between valence and arousal-relevant information (Kuppens et al., 2013).

text.text: Alternatively, this heterogeneity may reflect genuine differences in facial appearance that are captured by OpenFace but are less relevant to human judgments of perceptual similarity.
This possibility raises an important distinction between the physical features detected by computational models and the information prioritised by human observers.

text.text: One exception was smiling faces, which exhibited relatively consistent activation of AU06 (cheek raiser) and AU12 (lip corner puller), suggesting that OpenFace can recover coherent facial configurations despite naturalistic variability.

Moreover, the emergence of smiling faces as a distinct perceptual cluster, transcending differences in age and gender, suggests that smiles provide a particularly salient and consistent cue that observers spontaneously prioritise amid competing facial information (Peluso et al., 2025), rather than an artifact of experimentally constrained stimulus categories.

text.text: In sum, these findings suggest that the relationship between physical facial configurations and perceptual similarity is not uniform with some expressions, such as smiles, exhibiting coherence at both levels, whereas other perceptually similar faces may be supported by more heterogeneous combinations of facial features.

Our approach is not without limitations; we make no claim that our stimulus set represents the full spectrum of naturalistic facial attributes, and a different set of ambient faces could produce a distinct representational topography.
However, we intentionally chose a compact, highly diverse stimulus set in contrast to data-driven approaches operating at much larger, sparser scales (Bockes et al., 2025; Hebart et al., 2020).

text.text: Accordingly, future work should prioritize testing non-Western cohorts and scaling this paradigm to larger stimulus sets to determine how broadly this representational geometry generalizes.

While traditional approaches to face perception have often sought to minimise stimulus variability, our findings demonstrate that naturalistic faces can elicit remarkably consistent and reliable perceptual judgments, even across observers aged 20 to 76 years of age.
These findings suggest that the challenge for understanding face perception is not simply to control variability, but to identify the perceptual regularities that emerge despite it.
This distinction has important implications for both computational models and applied measures of social cognition.

For example, incorporating the multidimensional structure of naturalistic face representations into computational models may help develop more robust and generalisable facial analysis tools, with potential implications for reducing bias in automated decision-making.

Similarly, conventional clinical assessments of social cognition often rely on posed facial expressions and forced-choice categorisation tasks, which may not adequately capture how individuals interpret complex or ambiguous facial information in everyday life.

Establishing perceptual benchmarks grounded in naturalistic face similarity judgments may therefore provide a more ecologically valid framework for evaluating individual differences in social cognition (Henry et al., 2023).

text.text: Taken together, we demonstrate that humans spontaneously and flexibly combine broad categories and fine-grained dimensions to evaluate naturalistic faces.

By advancing a new methodological framework that accommodates variation in both facial information and observer behavior, this work moves beyond traditional stimulus rewilding (Dawel et al., 2025; Peluso, Long et al., 2023; Peluso et al., 2025) toward data-driven paradigms that allow the complex, flexible structure of face representations to guide more veridical models for describing how faces invite real-world meaning.
